carbonateBudget.title: A reef is a balance sheet
carbonateBudget.subtitle: Builders add limestone; grazers and borers take it away. The sign of the difference decides whether the platform rises.

hint.accreting: Calcification outruns erosion. Limestone accumulates, the platform grows, and it keeps pace with the sea.
hint.eroding: Erosion outruns calcification. The framework breaks down faster than it forms — the foundation itself is being spent.

carbonateBudget.units: kg CaCO₃ per m² per year. Healthy reefs sit near +4 to +10; below roughly 10–15% live cover the budget flips negative.

aragoniteThreshold.title: When the water stops letting a skeleton form
aragoniteThreshold.subtitle: More CO₂ in the air means less carbonate in the sea. Below a threshold, limestone dissolves faster than reefs can lay it down.

hint.accreting: The water is supersaturated with aragonite; corals spend energy but the skeleton holds and grows.
hint.dissolving: Saturation has fallen through the accretion floor. Bare framework now dissolves into the sea faster than it forms.

oceanColumnExplorer.title: A vertical ocean
oceanColumnExplorer.subtitle: Move through the water column; switch the circulation regime.

hint.stratified: A strong density boundary keeps the bright surface apart from the nutrient-rich interior.
hint.upwelling: Rising water lifts the nutrient boundary, but it does not bring sunlight into the abyss.

oceanColumnExplorer.aria: Ocean column in a {regime} regime with the probe at {depth} percent depth

zoneNote.surface: Light is abundant; nutrients can run short.
zoneNote.transition: Temperature and density change quickly here.

coastalUpwellingExplorer.title: Make the water climb
coastalUpwellingExplorer.subtitle: Alongshore wind and planetary rotation decide whether surface water leaves or piles against the coast.

hint.upwelling: Surface water moves offshore. Continuity replaces it with water from beneath the pycnocline.
hint.downwelling: Surface water moves toward the coast, piles up, and is forced downward.

result.productive: Nutrients can re-enter the sunlit layer.
result.suppressed: The nutrient boundary is pushed deeper.

jetVersusFoil.title: Two ways to push water
jetVersusFoil.subtitle: A siphon throws a little water very fast. A wing moves a lot of water gently. Only one of them is affordable all day.
jetVersusFoil.footnote: A siphon this efficient would need an aperture of {area} cm² — by then it is a wing.

readout.wastedNote: Power that moved water, not the animal
readout.costNote: The siphon costs {factor}× as much per metre

hint.competitive: At this aperture the siphon is no longer losing — but an opening this wide is a fin with a hole in it, not a nozzle.
hint.penalised: The siphon burns {factor}× the energy per metre travelled. Sustainable for seconds, not for an ocean crossing.

jetVersusFoil.units: Cost of transport in joules per kilogram per metre. Measured values: cephalopods 1.5–4.5, fishes and rays 0.2–0.6.

cavitationCeiling.title: How fast you may swim depends on how deep you are
cavitationCeiling.subtitle: Push a fin too hard in shallow water and the water tears into bubbles. Pressure at depth makes that impossible.

band.dolphin: Measured surface limit for dolphins and fast fish

readout.safeDepthNote: Shallowest depth this burst stays clean
readout.verdictNote: Bubble collapse pits skin at gigapascal pressures

hint.cavitating: This burst would cavitate here. The same speed becomes safe below about {depth} m, where ambient pressure holds the water together.
hint.clean: No bubbles at this depth. The deep ocean is where a high-speed jet stops being self-destructive.

cavitationCeiling.units: Cavitation number σ = (p∞ − p_v) / (½ρU²); onset near 0.5–1.2 depending on the surface geometry.
cavitationCeiling.aria: At {depth} m the cavitation-free speed ceiling is {ceiling} metres per second.

pressureDoesNotCrush.title: What deep water actually breaks
pressureDoesNotCrush.subtitle: Being crushed is the famous danger and the one that never happens. The real limits are molecular, and one of them is a wall.

rowNote.crush: volume lost by a gas-free body
rowNote.enzyme: reaction speed left, relative to the surface
rowNote.membrane: unsaturated lipid needed to stay fluid

readout.osmoticNote: Bony fish run out at about {depth} m

hint.withinCeiling: Pressure is doing nothing mechanical. It is slowing enzymes and stiffening membranes, and there are still {headroom} mOsm of osmotic room before the biochemical wall.
hint.pastCeiling: Past this depth the protectant that keeps proteins folded would make the animal saltier than the sea. This is where bony fish stop being found — not because they are crushed, but because they cannot hold their water.

pressureDoesNotCrush.aria: At {depth} m the pressure is {pressure} megapascals.

abyssalSignalStack.title: A skin that talks in a room with no light
abyssalSignalStack.subtitle: Three of its four layers can only work by reflecting light. Take the light away and only the last one still says anything.

modeNote.crypsis: Emission suppressed and pigment contracted: an ultra-black surface that gives a searching predator's beam nothing to come back with.
modeNote.chatter: Waves of light run across the mantle at millisecond speed — coordinating the hunt and disorienting whatever is being hunted.
modeNote.counterlight: Belly photophores match the faint glow still coming down from above, erasing the silhouette from anything looking up.

tierNote.chromatophore: pigment sacs pulled open by muscle

readout.blueNote: The only window the sea keeps open
readout.redNote: Gone in the first few tens of metres
readout.channelNote: Which layer can still be seen

hint.reflective: There is still enough light down here for pigment and mirrors to show contrast — about {pct}% of the usable range remains.
hint.emissive: Reflective layers have nothing left to reflect. Anything this animal wants to say from here down, it has to say by making light itself.

abyssalSignalStack.aria: At {depth} m, {reflective}% of the reflective signalling range remains.

ventEnergyBudget.title: Can a vent field pay for this animal?
ventEnergyBudget.subtitle: Productivity per square metre is rainforest-grade. The trouble is the number of square metres, and the four steps between.
ventEnergyBudget.scaleNote: tier widths on a log scale — kg carbon per year at right

readout.maxResidentNote: Living here year-round on this field alone

hint.sufficient: At these settings the field could carry the pack — but it takes numbers no measured vent field has produced.
hint.deficit: The field falls short by a factor of about {shortfall}. The biggest animal it could keep permanently weighs {resident} kg, so a multi-tonne pack has to be eating somewhere else.

ventEnergyBudget.earthCheck: Earth's real vent residents match this: eelpouts under 1 kg, crabs under 0.5 kg, the vent octopus under 0.2 kg. Nothing large lives at a vent.
ventEnergyBudget.aria: Trophic pyramid delivering {apex} kg carbon per year to the apex tier, against a pack demand of {demand} kg per year.

thermalScope.title: Cold water charges in two currencies
thermalScope.subtitle: Speed sags gently in the cold. Reaction time collapses — and a coordinated strike is a timing problem first.
thermalScope.footnote: power scales as speed cubed; twitch rate scales directly

readout.verdictImpossible: Out of reach at any plausible heat retention

hint.capable: Fast enough, and — the part that matters — able to decide fast enough. Every animal in the pack can commit inside the same window.
hint.tooSlow: The speed is survivable; the reaction time is not. Closing the gap needs roughly +{needed} °C of retained metabolic heat, which on Earth means counter-current vessel bundles.

thermalScope.earthCheck: Tunas and lamnid sharks hold swimming muscle and braincase 5–15 °C above the water using retia mirabilia. No cephalopod on Earth does.
thermalScope.aria: Muscle at {temp} °C gives a strike latency of {latency} milliseconds.

hydrostaticDepth.title: The same depth, two different weights of water
hydrostaticDepth.subtitle: Pressure is the weight of the water overhead, so weaker gravity means every threshold sits deeper.
hydrostaticDepth.residualLabel: Residual volume — the lung can go no smaller

verdict.squeeze: Below residual volume — chest wall alone cannot hold

hint.safe: The chest is compressing but the air inside it still has room to give. Nothing here needs anything unusual of the body.
hint.narcosis: Dissolved nitrogen has reached the pressure where it starts dissolving into nerve membranes: slowed thought, clumsy hands, an unearned sense of calm.
hint.squeeze: The air is squeezed below the volume the chest can physically fold to. Without more than a litre of blood shifting into the lungs to fill the gap, the vessels tear.

hydrostaticDepth.assumption: Seawater density is assumed to match Earth's 1025 kg/m³ — canon never states Pandora's.
hydrostaticDepth.narcosisNote: On this world, nitrogen turns narcotic at about {n} m.
hydrostaticDepth.aria: Lung volume against depth at {depth} metres and {atm} atmospheres

diveOxygenBudget.title: A breath-hold is a division problem
diveOxygenBudget.subtitle: Oxygen carried, divided by oxygen spent. Where the body keeps that oxygen matters more than how much air it swallowed.
diveOxygenBudget.barTitle: Where the oxygen is kept — lungs, blood, muscle

verdict.aerobic: The dive fits inside the aerobic limit
verdict.anaerobic: Past the limit — the muscles go anaerobic

hint.aerobic: Everything this dive costs is paid out of oxygen the body brought with it. Surface, breathe twice, go again.
hint.anaerobic: The muscles have run out of their own oxygen and switched to burning sugar without it. The acid stays trapped in the legs until surfacing, then floods in — and the next dive has to wait.

diveOxygenBudget.derivedNote: No measured diving metabolic rate exists for these animals in the source, so the rate is set here and calibrated against an untrained human's known limit.
diveOxygenBudget.aria: Aerobic dive limit against body mass, currently {minutes} minutes

adaptationTimescale.title: How long does a body need?
adaptationTimescale.subtitle: Every change to a diving body has a clock. Give it a month and one set of things becomes possible; give it a million years and another.

verdict.none: Not even a reflex has settled
verdict.acclimatization: Reversible — and it fades if the pressure lifts
verdict.plasticity: Grown in during childhood, kept for life
verdict.genetic: Only across generations, never within one body
verdict.skeletal: Deep time, and no going back

hint.none: Too little time for anything to change. Even the spleen's response needs days of repetition before it starts arriving reliably.
hint.acclimatization: This is tuning, not rebuilding: the same body running different settings. It is also the tier that disappears — Korean divers lost their raised winter metabolism within two or three years of putting on wetsuits.
hint.plasticity: Long enough for a growing body to be shaped by what it does. Untrained children given a month of practice matched sea-nomad children's underwater eyesight exactly — and kept it. Nothing was inherited; something was learned deeply enough to stay.
hint.genetic: Now we have left the individual behind. Enlarged spleens in a diving population show up in divers and non-divers alike, which is what makes them inheritance rather than training — and that signal needs tens to hundreds of generations of pressure.
hint.skeletal: This is the only tier that can turn a tail into a fluke, and it takes millions of years. No amount of practice reaches it, which is exactly why the anatomy is the part a newcomer cannot train into.

adaptationTimescale.generationNote: Generation length converts the two inherited traits from generations into calendar time; the placements are order-of-magnitude, not exact dates.
adaptationTimescale.aria: Adaptation timescale ladder with {count} of {total} traits within reach

ascentHypoxia.title: The danger is on the way up
ascentHypoxia.subtitle: Oxygen pressure rises going down and collapses coming back. The urge to breathe tracks carbon dioxide, which is the wrong alarm.

verdict.warned: The alarm arrives before the oxygen runs out
verdict.blackout: Oxygen fails before any warning comes

hint.safe: Short enough and slow enough that oxygen pressure never falls through the floor, even as the lungs re-expand on the way up.
hint.warned: The carbon dioxide alarm fires while there is still oxygen in reserve. This is the ordering the body is built for: the diver is uncomfortable, and therefore alive.
hint.blackout: Look at when the alarm arrives — after the oxygen already gave out. Hyperventilating added almost no oxygen to blood that was already saturated; all it removed was the warning. The diver never felt anything wrong.

ascentHypoxia.modelNote: An illustrative single-compartment model: the thresholds are measured values, the consumption rate is yours to set.
ascentHypoxia.aria: Oxygen pressure across a {seconds} second breath-hold dive
